ranges.en: Mishna example: slaughter in the south or blood collected in the south still leaves the offering subject to misuse.
Same rule applies to altered timing, and to slaughter with improper intent or outside the designated area.
Rabbi Yehoshua's principle: no misuse liability for an offering that once had a period of fitness for priests.
Offerings that never had a fit period for priests remain consecrated, so benefit from them incurs misuse liability.
Which offerings had a period of fitness for priests?
Examples: meat left overnight, ritual impurity, or leaving the courtyard, all after consumption was permitted.
Which offerings never had a period of fitness for priests?
Examples: improper intent or wrong time or place, or collection by unfit people, all before consumption was permitted.
The Gemara notes the Mishna teaches misuse liability for most sacred offerings slaughtered in the south.
The Gemara asks why this needs stating, since southern slaughter seems not to remove misuse status.
The case had to be stated, because one might otherwise reason from a ruling already given.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yohanan that dead offerings are excluded from misuse by Torah law.
By analogy, a most sacred offering slaughtered in the south is like a strangled animal and so exempt.
The Mishna teaches that dead offerings were never fit at all, so the analogy fails.
Southern slaughter is unfit for most sacred offerings but still fit for lesser offerings, so it differs from death.
Why did the Mishna need to list all of these different cases?
Had the Mishna taught only south slaughter with northern collection, one might exclude the reverse case.
Northern slaughter with southern collection would seem exempt since collection is the weightier rite, so the case is needed.
Had only night slaughter with day collection been taught, one might think daytime is a valid time for sacrifice.
Day slaughter with night sprinkling would be exempt since night is not a valid time, so the case is taught separately.
Had only night slaughter with day sprinkling been taught, one might think day collection keeps misuse liability.
Day slaughter with night sprinkling is like a strangled animal, so it has no misuse liability, and the Mishna needed to say so.
The Mishna teaches the case of slaughter outside its time and outside its place.
For what purpose are such offerings fit?
They are fit because their sprinkling makes them subject to piggul, so they keep their consecrated status.

ranges.en: A dilemma: if disqualified offerings already ascended the altar, must they come back down?
Rabba holds that offerings which ascended the altar must descend.
Rav Yosef holds that offerings which ascended the altar do not descend.
On Rabbi Yehuda's view the dilemma need not be asked, since both Sages agree the offerings descend.
The Sages disagree only on Rabbi Shimon's view, and Rav Yosef follows Rabbi Shimon's straightforward reading.
Rabba objects that Rabbi Shimon's ruling is limited to particular cases and not general.
The cases Rabbi Shimon addresses are those where blood was placed above or below the red line incorrectly.
Rabbi Shimon speaks only of offerings slaughtered properly in the north and collected in the north.
Offerings slaughtered in the south count as strangled, so Rabbi Shimon would agree they descend.
The Mishna teaches misuse liability for offerings slaughtered in the south, which seems to conflict with Rabba.
The Mishna fits Rav Yosef's view, but for Rabba the liability seems difficult to explain.
What does the Mishna's phrase about liability for misuse mean?
It means liability by rabbinic law.
What practical difference is there between Torah and rabbinic misuse?
Torah misuse requires paying the additional one-fifth, while rabbinic misuse does not.
Is there such a thing as rabbinic misuse of consecrated property?
Yes, as Ulla taught.
Ulla teaches that Rabbi Yohanan said dead offerings are excluded from Torah misuse.
Since they are excluded only by Torah law, they fall under rabbinic misuse, and so do offerings slaughtered in the south.
If the Mishna already taught this, why does Ulla need to repeat it?
Ulla's statement was needed, since people would not distance themselves from southern offerings, which look properly sacrificed.
Dead offerings are different, since people distance themselves from them, so one might exclude them from rabbinic misuse.
Ulla teaches that dead offerings are also subject to rabbinic misuse.
A mishna teaches that a dead sin offering used for benefit incurs misuse liability, which suggests the point was already taught.
Might one think the mishna's rule already covers Ulla's point, making his statement unnecessary?

ranges.en: A dead sin offering is treated differently, since people shun it once it can no longer atone, so the Sages needed no decree.
Ulla teaches that other dead most sacred animals still fall under misuse by rabbinic decree.
Is a dead sin offering subject to the laws of misuse at all?
A baraita teaches that sin offerings left to die, and money going to the Dead Sea, may not be benefited from but do not incur misuse.
Those offerings are shunned even while alive, so no decree was needed, unlike a sin offering that was fit during its lifetime.
Rav Yosef raises an objection against Rabba by combining several sources.
A mishna on bird offerings disqualified by pinching or wrong sprinkling says they do not impart impurity to garments, yet misuse applies.
The mishna excludes a bird sin offering performed correctly below the red line, which is permitted to priests.
Another mishna distinguishes birds disqualified inside the sacred area, which do not impart impurity, from those disqualified outside it, which do.
A third mishna states that offerings disqualified inside the sacred area do not descend once they ascend the altar.
Rav Yosef concludes that this refutes Rabba's view.
Rabbi Elazar holds the disputed case is obvious, citing a burnt offering of a private altar brought into the courtyard.

ranges.en: Once the partitions admit the offering, it has the status of a burnt offering in the Temple in all respects.
Rabbi Elazar asks about a private-altar burnt offering disqualified by southern slaughter whose limbs ascended the altar: must they descend?
Since Rabbi Elazar asked only one of the two cases, the other must be obvious to him, which would settle whether he follows Rabba or Rav Yosef.
The inference is rejected: Rabbi Elazar may have been unsure of that case too, and he raised one question based on the other.
Even following Rabba, his view applies only when the offering was consecrated for the Temple courtyard, not for a private altar.
Alternatively, even Rav Yosef's view may apply only to offerings consecrated properly, so the question remains open and stands unresolved.
Rav Giddel reports Rav's ruling: piggul intent in sprinkling does not remove sacred meat from misuse, nor bring lesser offerings into misuse.
Abaye sat and taught this ruling of Rav Giddel.
Rav Pappa raises an objection to Abaye.
A mishna on the thanks offering states that slaughter outside the wall keeps the loaves unsanctified.
The mishna continues: loaves are sanctified when the thanks offering was disqualified by piggul intent or by being outside its area.
The objection: this shows piggul in slaughter brings lesser offerings into misuse, contradicting Rav's ruling.
Abaye was silent and could not answer, so he brought the difficulty to Rabbi Abba.
Rabbi Abba answers that the mishna concerns piggul intent in slaughter, while Rav's ruling concerns piggul intent in sprinkling.
Rav Ashi challenges Rava, asking whether this explanation conflicts with another ruling.
Ulla teaches that a piggul handful brought to the altar has its piggul status lapse once it is burned.
Since removing the handful is equivalent to slaughter in animal offerings, the same should apply: slaughter alone with piggul intent would make it piggul.
Rava replies that Ulla meant a prohibited act brings the offering toward piggul, but full piggul requires improper intent at the rite equivalent to sprinkling.

ranges.en: Ulla's teaching about a handful making the rest piggul seems to imply that slaughter alone with piggul intent also suffices.
Ulla's point is not that intent alone makes it piggul, but that a prohibited act starts the process, and full piggul needs improper intent at the rite.
Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing Ilfa's view.
Ilfa holds that the dispute over piggul versus disqualification applies to intents in two different rites.
Ilfa's example: one slaughters the first organ with piggul intent beyond its time, then the second organ with intent outside its place.
When both intents fall in one rite, everyone including Rabbi Yehuda agrees it is a mixture of intents and the offering is not piggul.
Rav Giddel agrees: piggul is revealed only at sprinkling, so one rite means not piggul, while two rites follow the dispute.
If so, the thanks offering case should also become piggul only after sprinkling, and so Rav Giddel's view seems inconsistent with the loaves ruling.
Sanctified here means only that the loaves can be disqualified and need burning, not that misuse applies.
A baraita states that a piggul offering always incurs misuse liability, which might support Rav Giddel.
The baraita cannot be proof, since if its blood was not yet sprinkled the offering would be subject to misuse anyway.
The baraita may concern sprinkled blood, but it refers to a burnt offering, which is always subject to misuse, so it does not prove the point.
If the baraita concerns a burnt offering, the ruling is obvious, since it wholly belongs to God.

ranges.en: The latter clause of a baraita holds that an offering whose blood was left overnight remains subject to misuse even after later sprinkling.
If the baraita concerns a sin offering, its ruling makes sense: overnight blood keeps it subject to misuse.
If it concerns a burnt offering, the ruling would be superfluous, since burnt offerings are always subject to misuse.
The latter clause supports Rav Giddel, so perhaps the first clause also supports him.
That is rejected: the latter clause is not certain to support Rav Giddel, since sprinkling after piggul may differ from overnight blood.
The difference: overnight blood is a failure of action, which sprinkling cannot cure, whereas piggul is only a matter of intent, which sprinkling may cure.
A baraita states that a piggul most-sacred offering incurs misuse liability, which might support Rav Giddel.
No proof: the baraita may refer to a case where the blood was not yet sprinkled.
If the blood was sprinkled, is the offering exempt from misuse, and then why does the latter clause mention lesser offerings?
The baraita should have drawn the distinction within most-sacred offerings; that the latter clause supports Rav Giddel still holds.
If the latter clause supports Rav Giddel, the first clause may as well.
Not necessarily: lesser offerings are a clear case, while most-sacred offerings depend on the sprinkling.
Rabbi Yehoshua's principle: no misuse liability for an offering that had a period of fitness for priests, and liability for one that never had it.
Which offering had a period of fitness for priests?
One whose meat remained overnight, became impure, or left the courtyard after being sacrificed properly.
Which offering never had a period of fitness for priests?
One slaughtered with improper intent or outside its time or place, or whose blood was collected and sprinkled by unfit people.
Bar Kappara tells bar Pedat to study the question he will ask him tomorrow in the study hall.
Does Rabbi Yehoshua's fitness refer to the fitness of slaughter, as it was taught in the study hall?

ranges.en: Is the phrase fitness referring to fitness of sprinkling or fitness of eating the meat?
Hizkiyya holds the phrase refers to fitness of slaughter, while Rabbi Yohanan holds it refers to fitness of eating.
Rabbi Zeira objects that the mishna does not precisely match either Hizkiyya or Rabbi Yohanan.
The mishna's examples, such as meat left overnight after blood was properly sprinkled, show the offering is not liable despite the blood still being unsprinkled.
So we learn that the phrase refers to fitness of sprinkling.
Rejected: the mishna concerns meat left overnight after the blood was sprinkled, so the phrase refers to fitness of eating.
The mishna lists unfit offerings: wrong intent, wrong place or time, or blood collected and sprinkled by unfit people.
What circumstances does the mishna mean by collection and sprinkling by unfit people, since disqualification would need only one act?
Rather, the mishna concerns collection by unfit people with sprinkling by fit people, since this alone leaves the offering liable.
So we learn that the phrase refers to fitness of sprinkling, as the offering is exempt before the blood is actually sprinkled.
Rav Yosef objects: this reading conflicts with a mishna on laundering garments that concerns unfit collection and sprinkling in either order.
A disqualified sin offering's blood needs no laundering whether or not it had a period of fitness.
Which sin offering had a period of fitness and was later disqualified?
One left overnight, rendered impure, or that left the courtyard.
Which sin offering never had a period of fitness?
One slaughtered outside its place or time, or whose blood was collected by unfit people and sprinkled.
What are the circumstances of this mishna's case?
If the blood was collected and sprinkled by unfit people, it needs no laundering, so the reverse would need laundering, which is an untenable inference.
A verse on laundering blood of a sin offering applies only to unsprinkled blood, so the mishna's wording is not exact.

ranges.en: Rav Asi asserts the mishna is not meant exactly, so its wording cannot be relied on.
Rav Asi asks why the tanna would teach two mishnayot imprecisely.
Rather, only one mishna is imprecise, so the other is precise and its wording is meaningful.
The Zevachim mishna teaches that an unfit priest collecting blood renders the remainder leftovers.
Asks the reason why the sprinkling of a fit priest counts for nothing.
Because the blood has become leftovers, so a later sprinkling has no effect.
Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yohanan is cited as a challenge to the claim that unfit sprinkling creates leftovers.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that only sprinkling with piggul intent, beyond time or place, renders the remainder leftovers.
Objection: Rabbi Yohanan's wording implies an unfit priest's sprinkling does not render leftovers, contradicting Rav Asi.
Rejects that inference: even an unfit priest's sprinkling renders the blood leftovers.
Objection from a broader formulation of Rabbi Yohanan's ruling that seems to limit leftovers to those two cases.
Explains Rabbi Yohanan's ruling as limited to community offerings, so an impure priest still renders leftovers.
Other invalid sprinklings, such as a blemished priest's, do not render the blood leftovers in community offerings.
Brings a baraita stating that piggul offerings remain subject to misuse, to test the reading of the mishna.
Suggests the baraita refers to collecting blood with piggul intent, implying proper collection removes misuse.
Rejects the inference: the baraita may concern a piggul offering whose blood was already sprinkled.
Asks what the baraita teaches if it is not about collection.
The baraita teaches Rav Giddel's view that piggul sprinkling keeps an offering subject to misuse.

ranges.en: Brings a baraita of Rabbi Shimon distinguishing notar cases that are liable for misuse from those that are not.
The baraita explains that consumption before sprinkling creates liability, while consumption after sprinkling does not.
Infers from the baraita that merely collecting the blood, without sprinkling, does not remove misuse liability.
Concludes that fitness for eating the meat, not fitness for sprinkling, is the criterion in the mishna.
Rejects the inference: the baraita concerns blood collected shortly before sunset, when sprinkling was impossible.
Objects that by the same logic a case with time to sprinkle would not be liable, which seems wrong.
Asks why Rabbi Shimon taught this distinction rather than a more precise one about collection before or after sunset.
Answers that Rabbi Shimon's point is before fitness for sprinkling liability applies, and after fitness it does not.
Brings a second baraita about piggul offerings, where misuse liability depends on whether sprinkling occurred.
The second baraita explains that eating before sprinkling creates liability, while eating after sprinkling does not.
Infers from the piggul baraita that the fitness of eating the meat, not sprinkling, governs the mishna.
Concludes that the baraita teaches that fitness for consumption is the criterion.
Rejects the inference: the baraita refers to blood collected too late in the day to be sprinkled.
Objects: if so, when there was time to sprinkle, the offering would be removed from misuse, which seems problematic.
Asks why the baraita states a distinction after sprinkling rather than a more precise one about collection timing.
Answers that Rabbi Shimon indeed means before fitness for sprinkling creates liability, and after it does not.
Brings a further baraita on piggul in offerings of the most sacred order and infers that eating fitness governs misuse.
Rejects this proof: the baraita may refer to a case where the priest did not yet sprinkle the blood.
Objects that if sprinkling was done, the baraita's contrast with lesser sanctity offerings would be unexplained.
Asks why the baraita contrasts sacred and lesser offerings rather than teaching the before and after sprinkling distinction.
Explains the baraita's wording: proper sprinkling brings an offering into misuse liability, while improper sprinkling can remove it.

ranges.en: The mishna states Rabbi Eliezer's view that sprinkling does not permit meat that left the courtyard, so misuse applies.
Rabbi Akiva's view: sprinkling is effective despite the meat leaving the courtyard, so misuse does not apply.
Rabbi Akiva cites the case of a substitute sin offering whose status shows how sprinkling affects a second animal.
Draws an a fortiori inference from that case to the meat of an offering that left the courtyard and returned.
The mishna extends the dispute to sacrificial portions of lesser offerings that left the courtyard before sprinkling.
States the two sages' views on lesser offerings: Eliezer denies misuse liability, while Akiva affirms it.
Asks why the mishna needs both disagreements when they seem to rest on the same principle.
Answers that both cases are needed, since each alone would imply a different limit on the effect of improper sprinkling.
Rabbi Yohanan explains Rabbi Akiva's view: sprinkling is effective only if part of the meat remained inside the courtyard.
Rav Asi reports that his Babylonian colleagues had already taught him the same version of this view.

ranges.en: A teaching holds that intent to consume lost or burned portions after their time renders an offering piggul.
Objects that lost and burned portions no longer exist, so the teaching seems to contradict Rabbi Yohanan's view.
Asks whether Rav Asi really held this, recalling his dilemma about intent regarding blood poured out the next day.
Rabbi Zeira cites a rule from Hullin that non-edible residue combines with meat for impurity, to resolve the dilemma.
Explains the contradiction: intent regarding blood that will be lost is ineffective, just like a fully departed offering.
Objects that the baraita's wording on lost and burned portions seems to allow intent even for destroyed portions.
Rava emends the baraita to refer only to portions that are about to be lost or burned but still exist.
Rav Pappa explains Rabbi Akiva's view: sprinkling helps only when the meat left and the blood remained inside.
Cites a baraita that supports Rav Pappa: if blood left the courtyard, a later sprinkling does nothing.
Rabbi Akiva supports his view with the case of a substitute sin offering, where the first sprinkling exempts the second.
Rabbi Elazar limits Rabbi Akiva's view to offerings slaughtered at the same time, not one after the other.
Introduces a report from Rabbi Shimon about an encounter in the village of Pani concerning Rabbi Akiva's view.
An old man asks Rabbi Shimon whether Rabbi Akiva really held that sprinkling helps meat that left the courtyard.
Rabbi Shimon confirms that Rabbi Akiva held this view.
Rabbi Shimon's Galilean colleagues object that sprinkling cannot make acceptable what is already unfit.
Rabbi Akiva replies that sprinkling does take effect even on unfit meat, asking whether his student does not agree.
Rabbi Akiva's example of the substitute sin offering shows that both offerings remain subject to misuse liability.
Concludes that if both animals were slaughtered and their blood set in cups, both remain subject to misuse.

ranges.en: Argues from the case of two sin offerings that sprinkling one exempts the other's meat, and by a fortiori, the meat that left the courtyard.
Reish Lakish reports that Rav Oshaya said Rabbi Akiva's reply to his student was deceptive, and explains why.
Objects that whether the offerings were slaughtered together or one after the other makes no difference, since the other is unfit either way.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that Reish Lakish himself accepts the distinction between offerings slaughtered together and separately.
Presents a case of two guilt offerings where the sacrificial portions were raised before sprinkling, and draws a conclusion.
Objects: if the two offerings form one entity, why must the portions raised before sprinkling descend?
Cites Ulla's teaching that lesser portions raised before sprinkling are not brought down, supporting the objection.
Reish Lakish is silent, so Rabbi Yohanan refutes his opinion decisively by raising the difficulty.
The mishna opens by stating that sprinkling of most sacred offerings has both lenient and stringent aspects, and lesser offerings only stringent.
Explains the most sacred offerings: before sprinkling the portions and meat are subject to misuse, and after it only the portions.
Explains lesser offerings: after sprinkling, the portions are subject to misuse and all prohibitions apply to both, so all aspects are stringent.
Asks why the priest may not eat the meat after sprinkling if it is his property, since the mishna only says no misuse.
Answers that the mishna's wording mirrors the first clause, so no prohibition on eating is implied.
Quotes the latter clause about lesser offerings and reads it as the Gemara's basis for the same inference.
Asks the same question about the meat of lesser offerings: why is it prohibited to the owners if it is their property?
Rabbi Hanina explains that the prohibition applies to meat removed before sprinkling, and that Rabbi Akiva's view covers leaving the courtyard for burning.

ranges.en: Even Rabbi Akiva concedes that sprinkling the blood of a bird offering does not make its meat permitted for eating; this closes the chapter.

Infers from the mishna's wording that the bird offering can be disqualified, yet cannot render other items impure.
Asks whose opinion the mishna expresses.
Answers that it is the Rabbis' view, citing a baraita in which Abba Shaul speaks of one who immersed that day.

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds that one who immersed that day renders sacred food impure, while the Rabbis hold he only disqualifies it.
Rava rejects the inference that the mishna follows the Rabbis, arguing it fits Abba Shaul and Rabbi Meir as well.
Rava explains that Rabbinic law gives one who immersed that day a lower level of impurity for consecrated food.
Asks why there is a prohibition on the sin offering's meat after sprinkling, if it is the priests' property.
Rabbi Hanina explains that the mishna concerns meat removed from its eating place, following Rabbi Akiva's view.
Rav Huna reports Rav's view that failing to squeeze out a bird sin offering's blood after sprinkling does not invalidate it.
Rav Adda bar Ahava reports Rav's contrary view: failure to squeeze out the blood invalidates the offering.
Cites the verse about squeezing out the remaining blood, which supports the view that squeezing is essential.
Asks what the verse means on Rav Huna's view, if squeezing is not essential.
Explains through a baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael that the verse requires squeezing only if blood remains.
Objects by analogy to the meal offering: if remainder suffices there, the same should hold here, even if none is left.

ranges.en: Cites a baraita on the meal offering's verse, showing that some of its flour, oil and frankincense must remain.
Explains that the meal offering is unique because the word leftover is repeated, so this rule does not apply to a bird sin offering.
Shmuel's father objects from a mishna on bird offerings, reading squeezing out the blood as a requirement for validity.
Resolves his own objection: the mishna's clauses address different cases, so squeezing matters only for the burnt offering.
Returns to the baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael: remaining blood must be squeezed out, but no remainder need be ensured.
Objects that the same school elsewhere holds failure to squeeze out the blood invalidates the offering, contradicting the baraita.
The mishna states that a bird burnt offering is subject to misuse until its ashes are taken to the ash heap, with karet liability after squeezing.
The mishna states the rules for burnt bulls and goats, including misuse liability on the flesh until it is fully scorched.
The mishna states that a burnt offering carries misuse liability for its flesh but not its hides, until removal to the ash heap.
The mishna states that sin, guilt and communal peace offerings carry misuse liability only for their portions on the altar.
The mishna states that the Shavuot loaves are subject to misuse until their blood is sprinkled, after which they are permitted.
The mishna states the shewbread's consecration and rules on its crust and arrangement on the Table.
The mishna states that the bowls of frankincense carry karet liability but no misuse once sacrificed.
The mishna states that meal offerings are subject to misuse from consecration and are disqualified by the usual factors.
The mishna states that after the handful is sacrificed, misuse liability applies to the handful until it reaches the ash heap.
Reports the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yohanan on whether one who benefits from the ash on the altar commits misuse.
Clarifies that both agree on misuse before the ashes are removed; the dispute concerns the period after removal.
Presents the two positions: Rav says the mitzva is complete, while Rabbi Yohanan says the ash stays consecrated.
Rabbi Yohanan derives his view from the verse on the priestly garments used to carry the ashes outside the camp.
Cites the mishna's wording about liability until the ash heap, which seems to contradict Rav's view.
Answers that Rav can read the mishna as referring to the time the ash is fit to be carried out, after the shovelful is removed.

ranges.en: Objects to Rav's explanation from a mishna: a dislodged ember is not restored, implying an ember on the altar must be restored.
Answers that an ember has substance and so remains fit for the altar, unlike ash, which Rav's view can accommodate.
Another Sage raises the objection in reverse, arguing that the mishna implies ash without substance carries no misuse liability.
Answers that Rabbi Yohanan can say the same about ash, and that the mishna names an ember to teach that even it is not restored.
Reports the dispute between Rav and Levi on where the value of misused meat goes: communal gift offerings or an entirely burnt item.
Cites a baraita that follows Levi, requiring that the money buy something wholly consumed on the altar, namely incense.
Cites a baraita that follows Rav, requiring different handling of misuse money for sin and guilt offerings.
The baraita continues with the general rule that misuse money for altar offerings buys altar items, and communal offerings go to gifts.
Objects that the baraita contradicts itself: the sin offering clause says cast into the Dead Sea, while the summary says buy altar items.

ranges.en: Reports Abaye's reading of the baraita: its first clause follows Rabbi Shimon and its latter clause follows the Rabbis.
Rava holds that all agree there is no misuse liability when meat became impure before sprinkling or portions were already on the altar.
Asks whether this ruling is obvious, since the one who benefited caused no loss to Temple property.
Answers that Rava needed to state it, lest one think the burning of impure meat or turning of portions counts as service.
Rava explains the baraita: money goes to gift offerings if the benefit was learned after atonement, since one may not set money aside to be lost.
The mishna lists meal offerings and incense consumed wholly on the altar, for which misuse liability applies from declared consecration.
Those items carry no piggul liability, though they are liable for notar and impurity once placed in a service vessel.
States the principle: items with permitting factors carry no piggul liability until those factors are sacrificed.
Items without permitting factors, such as the handful and frankincense, carry notar and impurity liability but no piggul liability.

ranges.en: Asks the source for the claim that notar and impurity liability apply to both kinds of sacred items.

Argues by a fortiori inference from piggul, then cites the verse on approaching sacred items to limit liability.
Rabbi Elazar asks whether anyone who merely touches an item is liable, and how the verse can be understood.
Explains the verse as referring to items fit to be sacrificed, so liability waits for permitting factors or service vessel consecration.
Closes the chapter and opens the mishna on the five sin offerings left to die and their status for misuse.

ranges.en: The mishna states that a found sin offering whose year passed renders exchanges substitutes and carries misuse liability.
Asks what distinguishes the first clause's three cases, which ignore atonement, from the latter clause's two cases.

Asks why the same halakha appears in tractate Temura and is repeated here.
Answers that Temura teaches it for substitution, while Me'ila teaches it for misuse liability.
The mishna on a nazirite's undesignated money, and the rules for the money of a deceased nazirite's offerings.
Reish Lakish objects that the tanna should teach the same rule for a pair of birds with undesignated money.
Rava responds that the cases differ: the Torah requires a peace offering for the nazirite, but not doves that are unfit.
The mishna of Rabbi Shimon on blood and libations, and the baraita on when blood emerging into the Kidron still carries liability.
Asks the reason of the Rabbis who hold blood carries no misuse liability despite its consecrated origin.
Ulla and Rabbi Yohanan derive the rule from verses on atonement, arguing blood's status is unchanged before and after atonement.
Proposes the opposite inference: if blood is misuse-liable before atonement, it should remain so after.
Rejects that suggestion: nothing whose mitzva has been performed should still carry misuse liability, though the Gemara questions why not.

ranges.en: Objects that the removal of ash from the altar is a case whose mitzva is done yet still carries misuse liability.
Answers that ash removal cannot be a model, since two verses that come as one teach nothing beyond themselves.
Objects: if the scapegoat limbs are not misusable, the two verses do not come as one, so the answer fails.
Answers that the ash removal and the High Priest's vestments are two verses that come as one, so the principle still holds.
Objects that Rabbi Dosa holds the vestments are reusable and not interred, so the same difficulty returns.
Answers that ash removal and the broken-neck heifer are two verses that come as one, both misusable after the mitzva.
Challenges the reply: it works only if two verses that come as one do not teach a common aspect.
Explains that exclusions in both verses, the broken neck and next to the altar, limit misuse after the mitzva to those cases.
Suggests the mishna may not follow Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, a suggestion that the Gemara then tests.
A baraita of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok: congealed libation wine from the drainpipes is burned in sanctity.
Asks from where the baraita derives the rule that burning must be in sanctity, since the verse speaks of pouring.
Ravina derives it by a verbal analogy between sanctity in libations and in leftover offerings.
Notes the baraita seems to hold that libations keep sanctity after descending, contradicting the mishna.
Reconciles by saying the mishna refers to libations that never reached the bottom of the drainpipes.
Offers an alternative version of the discussion, asserting the mishna follows Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok.
Rejects that version: Rabbi Elazar concedes no Torah-level misuse, and the verse is only a support.
The mishna on ash of the inner altar, Candelabrum wicks, and doves too young or too old, with their misuse rules.
The Gemara begins to ask why the inner altar ash is not misusable once moved, opening the next question.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks from where the inner altar's ashes are also subject to misuse, given the external altar's ash verse.
Rabbi Elazar derives the inner altar's ash placement from the verse about the crop placed in the place of the ashes.
Objects that both verses may refer to the external altar, leaving no source for the inner altar's ashes.
Answers that the extra phrase in the verse teaches that the inner altar's ashes are placed there too.
Asks from where the Candelabrum's ashes are also placed east of the altar.
The mishna records Rabbi Shimon's dispute over doves too young or pigeons too old, and explains his reasoning.
Asks why young doves differ from an animal not yet of age, which may be consecrated and tithed.
Answers that an animal can be consecrated because it is redeemable, but birds with blemishes cannot be redeemed.
Ulla reports Rabbi Yohanan's view that sacrificial animals that died are excluded from misuse by Torah law.
Rav Hisda objects: who would accept this, since the sanctity inherent in them has nowhere to go.
Ulla replies that the mishna's pigeons present the same difficulty, so Rav Hisda's objection applies to the mishna too.
Rav Hisda concedes the rabbinic prohibition but raises a new difficulty about items that become misusable later.
Asks whether blood is such a case: not misusable at first, but misusable after it emerges via the Kidron canal.
The Sages reply that this is no proof, since blood is misusable from the start.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav holds that one who lets blood from a sacrificial animal may not benefit and is liable for misuse of that blood.
Rav Hamnuna objects from the milk and dove eggs of consecrated animals, which are not misusable, so products seem to lack the status.
Rav answers that blood is distinct because the animal cannot exist without it, while milk is not so essential.
Rav Mesharshiyya objects from a baraita on dung of the most sacred offerings, which is not misusable either.
Asks why dung is not misusable, since like blood the animal cannot exist without it.
Answers that dung is food passing out of the body and replaced from outside, unlike blood, which is part of the body.
Notes that the baraita's ruling that the money goes to the treasury supports Rabbi Elazar's principle.
The mishna states that milk and eggs of consecrated animals are not misusable, and explains this for altar animals only.
Asks whether an animal consecrated for its sale value would have misusable milk or eggs, since it is not meant for the altar.
Rav Pappa answers that the mishna is incomplete: only an animal consecrated for the altar's inherent sanctity is exempt.
The mishna begins its next clause: any consecrated item fit for sacrifice on the altar.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna sets out categories of consecrated items and gives examples of cisterns, dovecotes and trees full of their contents.
If the container was consecrated empty and later filled, misuse applies to the container but not to its later contents.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees on growths of consecrated fields; the mishna then rules on offspring and suckling from consecrated animals.
Laborers may not eat consecrated figs they work with, and a cow threshing consecrated produce may not eat the vetch.
Asks from where the rules that a tithed or consecrated mother's offspring may not suckle are derived.
Rav Ahadvoi derives the rules by verbal analogy to the firstborn offering, showing the milk is also forbidden.
Asks the reason for the cow ruling, since the verse on laborers in the vineyard does not cover Temple produce.
Rav Ahadvoi cites the verse not to muzzle a threshing ox, which applies only to a non-sacred field.
Describes a case: threshing one's non-sacred kalilin in a consecrated field makes one liable for misuse.
Objects that misuse requires the consecrated item to be detached from the ground, while the field is the ground itself.
Ravina answers that the field's dust benefits the kalilin, so the detached dust is what is misused when threshing.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Roots of a non-sacred tree entering consecrated land, and vice versa, may not be used initially, but no misuse liability applies.
Spring water flowing from non-sacred land into consecrated land is restricted, but usable once it emerges outside the consecrated field.
Water drawn into a golden jug is not consecrated until poured into the service flask, which makes misuse liable.
Willow branches are forbidden before placement at the altar, but permitted afterward since their mitzva is fulfilled.
Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Tzadok reports that the elders used willow branches for lulavim even before placement.
Reish Lakish explains the mishna: no misuse liability for water in excess of three log, but liability for three log.
The Gemara objects that the mishna's latter clause implies liability applies even to three log, contradicting Reish Lakish.
Reish Lakish replies that the qualification applies only to the latter clause, so his view stands.
Rabbi Yohanan holds that one is liable for misuse of all the water, with no fixed measure.
The Gemara asks whether Reish Lakish really holds that the water libation has a fixed measure.
The Gemara cites a mishna on pouring Sukkot water outside the Temple to challenge the fixed-measure view.
Rabbi Yohanan relays Rabbi Elazar's derivation from Rabbi Akiva that water and wine libations are two distinct obligations.
Reish Lakish argues that since wine has a three-log measure, water should too.
The Gemara infers from this argument that Reish Lakish holds water has no measure, which seems to conflict with his stated view.
The Gemara answers that Reish Lakish spoke according to Rabbi Menahem Yodafa's explanation, so he does hold a measure.
The Gemara cites a mishna on a nest atop a consecrated tree, and the liability for a consecrated tree's produce.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Idol object broken by itself: Rabbi Yohanan forbids its benefit, while Reish Lakish permits it.
Rabbi Yohanan's reasoning: a gentile did not nullify the idol, so breakage alone does not remove its status.
Reish Lakish's reasoning: the owner would have nullified it on seeing it broken, since the idol could not save itself.
Reish Lakish raises a proof against Rabbi Yohanan from the mishna about the nest atop the tree.
The mishna cited: a consecrated tree's nest is forbidden initially, and the nest is dislodged by striking it with a pole.
Reish Lakish reads the mishna as permitting branches that broke off the worshipped tree itself, contrary to Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan answers that the mishna refers to a bird bringing branches from elsewhere, so there is no proof.
Reish Lakish rejects that answer: then why is the consecrated nest forbidden initially if built from outside material?
The Gemara resolves that the mishna concerns branches from the same tree, and growths after consecration.
The Gemara supports this reading as reasonable, since the tanna would hold growths of consecrated property are not misusable.
If the branches came from elsewhere, one would not need a pole to remove the nest, so the objection returns.
Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Yohanan's answer: the nest is dislodged to remove the chicks, which are hard to take without climbing.
Rabbi Yaakov rules that flying chicks are permitted in both cases, while eggs are forbidden in both.
Rav Ashi adds that young chicks still dependent on their mother are treated like eggs and forbidden.
Mishna: Temple treasurers buying logs are liable for the wood but not for sawdust or fallen leaves.
Shmuel teaches that Temple structures are built from non-sacred materials and consecrated only after completion.
Why are materials not consecrated immediately, given that money donated for maintenance is already sanctified?
The treasurer designates that the donor's sanctity applies to the finished structure, so the money is freed for wages.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection from a mishna on Shekalim: leftover incense was desacralized via wages, which suggests transferring its sanctity to the structure was not used.
Reply: the mishna concerns a time when no construction exists equal in value to the leftover incense.
Shmuel's ruling that a consecrated item redeemed for a tiny sum is valid seems to conflict with the proposed procedure.
Reply: Shmuel's ruling applies only after the fact, not as an ab initio practice for treasurers.
Rav Pappa's reason for building with non-sacred materials: artisans might sit on consecrated stones, misusing sacred property.
Objection from the mishna on logs bought by treasurers: why are they liable for wood if the same reasoning would apply to non-sacred logs?
Rav Pappa replies that the mishna concerns logs acquired for same-day use, so no one would sit on them; the chapter ends.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: altar-offering items and maintenance items combine to reach the misuse measure, and altar items alone combine for piggul, notar and impurity.
The Gemara asks why the mishna needs its first clause, if the latter clause already joins altar and maintenance items despite their different sanctity.
The first clause is needed because piggul, notar and impurity apply only to altar items, so the tanna separates the two clauses.
Rabbi Yannai holds that misuse liability by Torah law applies only to maintenance items and burnt offerings.
Rabbi Yannai's basis is the verse on misuse in sacred items of the Lord, read as limited to items uniquely for the Lord.
Objection: a mishna makes altar items join for misuse, and another makes disqualified most-sacred offerings liable, both apparently rabbinic only.
Objection from a mishna on a blemished sin offering and a baraita on the fat, suggesting Torah liability for altar items.
Objection: the tanna cites a verse as the source for the halakha, which seems to make it Torah law.
Reply: the verse is merely a support, not the actual source of the halakha.
Objection from Ulla quoting Rabbi Yohanan: dead sacrificial animals lose misuse liability by Torah law.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yohanan's case is, testing whether he means maintenance items or altar items.
If the case is maintenance items, even dead ones would remain liable, as with a garbage heap consecrated to maintenance.
So must the case be altar items, and does Rabbi Yannai hold they are subject to misuse by Torah law?
The school of Rabbi Yannai is reported to hold that the earlier formulation of his view was rejected.
The verse on misuse in sacred items teaches only maintenance items; altar items are derived from other verses.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: five items of a burnt offering and its accompaniments combine for misuse and piggul, and six items of a thanks offering combine.
Rav Huna's version of the mishna reads in the world rather than in the burnt offering.
Rava objects that the mishna lists six items for the thanks offering, so the world version cannot be right.
Rav Huna replies that the mishna should be taught as referring to the burnt offering.
A baraita already teaches that burnt-offering flesh and sacrificial portions combine for the olive-bulk rules.
The baraita distinguishes: this applies to burnt offerings but not to peace offerings.
Objection: peace offerings should be liable for piggul, notar and impurity too, as the mishna on piggul implies for all offerings.
Reply: the baraita concerns joining for sprinkling the blood, and only then for the eating prohibitions.
The baraita is attributed to Rabbi Yehoshua: fat and meat combine for burnt offerings, but not for other offerings.
What is the relevance of a meal offering, which does not require blood sprinkling, to this baraita?
Rav Pappa explains it refers to the meal offering of libations accompanying animal offerings.
Mishna: terumah, tithe-terumah, demai terumah, challah and first fruits combine for the additional fifth and prohibition, and piggul and notar combine.
What is the reason that all of these foods are called terumah?
Verses show challah and first fruits are called terumah, so the other items need no explanation.
Mishna on carcasses and repugnant creatures combining; Rav's statement on it opens here.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Carcasses combine only for impurity according to the plain reading, while Levi holds kosher and non-kosher carcasses combine for eating as well.
Rav Asi holds kosher and non-kosher carcasses are distinct, and the Gemara debates whether he disagrees with Rav about impurity.
A baraita says half an olive-bulk of a dead cow and of a live camel do not combine, implying dead ones would combine, which challenges Rav Asi.
Reply: the baraita should be read as implying live animals combine, following Rabbi Yehuda that a limb of a live animal is forbidden.
Objection: if dead carcasses do not combine, why choose the extreme case, and another baraita implies dead carcasses do combine.
Reply: that tanna holds one prohibition takes effect even over an existing prohibition, while Rav Asi does not, so no conflict.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav holds one is flogged for eating an olive-bulk of creeping animals, because the Torah uses the word eating for them.
A baraita quoted before Rabbi Yohanan, reading the verse on impurity, implies a lentil-bulk of creeping animals is liable, challenging Rav.
Reply: the baraita concerns dead creeping animals, which impart impurity by a lentil-bulk, while Rav speaks of live ones.
Abaye objects that Rav is citing the mishna, which makes carcasses combine into an olive-bulk, so Rav's ruling conflicts with the baraita.
Rav Yosef replies that the inference about the mishna is Abaye's own, and Rav stated an independent halakha.
An objection from a mishna on limbs of impure bodies: Rabbi Yohanan's distinction between impurity and flogging is challenged.
Rava resolves the conflict: Rabbi Yohanan's lentil-bulk rule applies only to the eight creeping animals the verse singles out.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that if creeping animals differ by type, the same distinction should apply between kosher and non-kosher animals.

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava explains that the juxtaposition of kosher and non-kosher animals to creeping animals concerns the general prohibition, not measures.
Mishna: blood and flesh of a creeping animal combine for impurity, and Rabbi Yehoshua sets a principle on when items join by impurity and measure.
Rav Zeira holds blood and flesh combine only when they come from the same creeping animal.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Hanina rejects this with a baraita: the plural hatemeim shows that such items join even from different animals.
Rav Yosef reconciles the two: the baraita concerns half-measures from a whole animal, while Rav Zeira concerns parts of one.
A baraita on blood spilled on a slope shows that whether one is impure depends on whether the blood is from a whole body or part.
Objection: the reading of part of it conflicts with Rabbi Hanina's report of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, so the distinction must be drawn differently.
Rabbi Matya ben Harash asks Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in Rome from where the blood of creeping animals is impure.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai replies from a verse on the impure creeping animals in Leviticus 11:29.
His students praise him, but Rabbi Matya says the source is a tradition from Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei.
Background: the government decreed Jews not to keep Shabbat, circumcise, or refrain from intercourse during menstruation.
Rabbi Reuven ben Isterobeli deceives the gentiles into nullifying the three decrees, and once discovered they reinstate them.

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposal that Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai go to Rome, with Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei accompanying him.
Rabbi Yosei objects that the Sages would not ask a father to hand over his son, and Rabbi Shimon responds that he will go and needs a companion.
Rabbi Yosei decides to go in place of his son, fearing Rabbi Shimon's temper with his quick-witted son, who is punished anyway.
Explanation of the punishment: a question about the blood of creeping animals was raised while they walked the road.
From where is the blood of a creeping animal impure?
Rabbi Elazar answers that the source is Leviticus 11:29, the impure creeping animals.
Rabbi Shimon says the answer shows Elazar is a scholar, but a student may not rule before his teacher, so he curses him.
A demon possesses the emperor's daughter, is expelled by Rabbi Shimon, and the emperor's decrees are torn up after a reward.
Rabbi Elazar's own testimony about seeing Yom Kippur blood on the Curtain in Rome supports the account of the story.
Mishna: piggul and notar do not join for impurity, and carcass flesh of different kinds does not join even for the lenient impurity.
Shmuel holds the non-joining applies only to rabbinic hand impurity, while piggul and notar do join for eating.
A baraita on Rabbi Eliezer's reading of Exodus 29:34 shows that any disqualified sacred food carries an eating prohibition.
Mishna listing the measures by which impure foods and liquids join for teruma disqualification and other Torah measures.
A baraita gives Rabbi Shimon's reason that food of second-degree impurity can make food of first-degree impure.
Objection: second-degree food cannot make food impure at first degree, so the reason is not possible.
Rava and Rav Ashi explain Rabbi Shimon: the second-degree food is impure only through first-degree food, so they share a source.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: orla fruit and diverse kinds join to reach the mixture measure, while Rabbi Shimon says they do not join.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Shimon needs joining at all, since a baraita says he holds any amount is flogged.
Mishna: garment, sack, hide and mat join together to reach the measure for impurity.
Rabbi Shimon is asked what the reason is for the joining.
Reason: each of these materials can become impure through a zav's seat.
A baraita: if one cut pieces from each material and sewed a garment, its minimum measure depends on whether it is for lying, sitting or holding.
What is the reason the holding garment is a garment?
Reish Lakish cites Rabbi Yannai: it serves to protect the hands of a weaver, and fig cutters use it similarly.
Chapter-closing formula that names the next chapter on the sacrifices of the altar.
Mishna: benefit worth a peruta from consecrated property creates misuse liability, with Rabbi Akiva and the Sages differing on damage, with examples.
A baraita states that Rabbi Akiva concedes to the Sages where the item can be damaged.
If they agree, where exactly do Rabbi Akiva and the Sages disagree?
Rava: they disagree about middle garments and fine malmala cloth, which are not depreciated by each use.
A baraita: the misuse law applies equally to a common person, a king and the anointed High Priest.
Verses using the word ma'al for deviation show that misuse is a general term that covers all such unfaithfulness.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse on the people going astray after the gods, read as a parallel for deviating from an item's intended use.
A baraita raises possible readings: liability without damage, liability for benefit without damage, items attached to ground, and agents.
Verbal analogy from the word sin in teruma and in misuse, deriving that misuse requires damage and benefit together, on detached items and by agents.
If the analogy only covers consumption, how is benefit from an item that cannot be damaged a misuse, and how do combined acts add up?
The verse on misuse using the inclusive word anyone teaches liability in any case, even split consumption.
Hypothetical analogy from teruma: the Torah does not join two separate eating acts, but the inclusive verse of misuse does.
From where is it derived that eating part of an olive-bulk today and the rest tomorrow combine for misuse?
Again the verse on misuse, with its inclusive language, teaches that such acts combine in any case.
Hypothetical analogy from teruma: damage and benefit occur together, so misuse should follow the same rule.
From where is it derived that consumption by one person and another combine, even across three years?
The inclusive verse of misuse, meaning in any case, teaches that they combine.
The baraita continues with a further analogy from teruma, which is cut off at this point.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita on when liability begins for moving Temple funds to other sacred uses: Rabbi Shimon says at once, Rabbi Yehuda says only after the blood is sprinkled.
The verse on misuse with its inclusive wording teaches liability in any case, as the baraita's source.
What else could one think, since the verse says anyone and the king and High Priest are plainly included?
The inclusion is needed lest the anointing oil verse exclude the king and High Priest as strangers to the oil.
The Gemara summarizes the analogies: misuse is like the sota, like idol worship, and like teruma, each fixing a principle.
Rav Kahana objects to Rav Zevid that gold can be damaged, as shown by the gold of Nun's daughter-in-law.
Rav Zevid replies that the gold was thrown away carelessly, and gold itself does not suffer immediate damage.
If the sin offering rule applies to an unblemished animal, why is it subject to misuse only upon damage, as with a gold cup?
Rav Pappa: the case is a blemished animal, which the treasury sells, so removing wool lowers its price and causes damage.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: repeated misuse counts only for an animal and service vessels, while Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says any non-redeemable consecrated item counts.
Whose opinion is the mishna? The Gemara identifies it as Rabbi Nehemiah's.
A baraita: repeated misuse applies only to an animal according to the first Tanna, and to service vessels according to Rabbi Nehemiah.
The first Tanna reads the verse on the ram of the guilt offering as concerning animals only.
Rabbi Nehemiah's a fortiori argument: if vessels sanctify other items, they themselves should be subject to repeated misuse.
Objection: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's rule seems identical to the first Tanna's, so why is it presented as dissent?
Rava replies there is a difference regarding donated wood, which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi treats as an offering.
A baraita on a vow to bring wood: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds wood is an offering requiring salt and waving.
Rava and Rav Pappa draw implications of that view: donated wood needs more wood and a handful removed first.
Rav Pappa notes a further difference for blemished consecrated animals that were slaughtered before redemption.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says such animals must be buried, while the Sages say they are redeemed.
Mishna: one who takes a consecrated stone or beam for his use is not liable for misuse.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: giving a consecrated item to another makes the giver liable, and consumption and benefit by different people combine to a peruta.
What is the difference between the one who keeps the item and the one who gives it, that only the giver is liable?
Shmuel: the case is a Temple treasurer who holds all consecrated property in his charge, so keeping it is not misuse.
Mishna: one who builds a consecrated beam into his house is not liable until he lives beneath it and derives a peruta of benefit.
Why is the residence condition needed, since building the item into the house already involves misuse?
Rav: the case is placing the beam on a window, where mere placement is not a change, so misuse starts only with residence.
The Gemara proposes a baraita's rule on prostrating before a house as support for Rav's view.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika rejects the support: the beam is liable on another principle, the visible benefit prohibition.
Another baraita on residing in a consecrated house is proposed as support for Rav's view.
Reish Lakish replies the baraita concerns a house built from items consecrated while detached, so Rav's view is not needed.
Objection: why does the baraita teach a cave rather than a stone house built and then consecrated, which would be the clearer case?
The tanna chose the cave because it is conclusive, while a consecrated house is not always exempt.
Chapter-closing formula, naming the next chapter on the agent who performs his agency.
Mishna: if an agent performs his agency properly the homeowner is liable; if not, the agent is liable, with examples on meat and liver.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Which tanna holds that any matter an agent would consult about counts as two separate items for misuse?
Rav Hisda rejects that answer: the mishna cannot follow Rabbi Akiva's view on vows about gourds versus vegetables.
Abaye replies that even Rabbi Akiva would require consultation, so the agent who acted alone did not perform his agency.
Who is the tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Akiva in the Nedarim mishna?
A baraita on vows about meat: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits head, feet, innards and birds, and treats innards as not meat.
Why does the first tanna count bird meat as meat, while fish is distinct, if an agent would also say he could not find animal meat?
Rav Pappa: the case is a day of bloodletting, when people avoid fish, so the agent would not consult about buying fish.
If so, bird meat would also be avoided after bloodletting, as Shmuel's statement suggests.
A baraita: one does not let blood before eating fish, birds or salted meat, supporting the concern about bloodletting.
Rav Pappa's second explanation: the case is a day when the eyes hurt, when people avoid fish, so no consultation occurs.
The mishna's ruling is taken to show that an agent who adds to his agency remains an agent, making the owner liable too.
Rav Sheshet objects that the inference is not necessary, since the agent may have said he acted partly on his own intent.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Sheshet explains the mishna's teaching: without it one might think the agent uproots the owner's agency by adding to instructions.
Mishna: agents who fetch from the wrong place, minors or the mentally impaired sent to buy, and the owner's remedy of desacralizing the money.
What is the mishna teaching us by saying that unspoken matters in the heart are not significant?
Unspoken desires in the heart are not matters, so the owner is liable, not the agent.
Objection: deaf-mutes, imbeciles and minors cannot be agents at all, so how can the owner be liable for their performance?
Rabbi Elazar: the Sages treat these people like a vat of olives, whose moisture is wanted by the owner, so their acts count as intended.
A mishna on Teharot: olives become susceptible to impurity from the moisture that leaks into the vat, not the basket, as the owner intends it.
Rabbi Yohanan cites a baraita on an eiruv placed on a monkey or elephant, showing agency performed by unfit agents is valid.
Case: money sent with a competent person, where the agent did not remember that it was consecrated.
A baraita contradicts: if the owner remembered and the agent did not, the agent is liable, and if both remembered, the storekeeper is.
Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction: the mishna concerns the case where both the agent and the owner remembered.
Mishna on lamps and wicks, etrogim, and a gold dinar for a robe, with Rabbi Yehuda's dissent on liability.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's case: an agent bought a robe and a cloak for three sela each, and both are liable for misuse.
Rabbi Yehuda rules the homeowner is not liable, since the agent brought a smaller, inferior robe than requested.
The Gemara infers from the mishna the resolution that a partial performance of agency still transfers the part acquired.
Some say this inference cannot be drawn from the mishna, because its case is dissimilar.
What exactly are the circumstances of the mishna being discussed?
The mishna's case is an agent who brought a robe worth six sela for three, so the homeowner received what he wanted.
If so, the latter clause of Rabbi Yehuda would not make sense, since the homeowner did not receive exactly what he asked for.
Rabbi Yehuda means the homeowner could have said that with the full dinar a finer robe worth two dinars could have been bought.
The latter clause supports this reading, since it teaches that Rabbi Yehuda concedes the legume case where both are liable.
How can this be: if the place sells legumes at market rate and a seller discounts more for a larger payment, why is the legume case different?
Rav Pappa says it is a place where goods are sold by bundles, and the case of a single coin is different there.
Mishna: one who deposits money with a money-changer may not use bundled coins; if he uses them, he is liable.
If the coins are unbundled, the depositor may use them, so if he spends them he is not liable.
A householder's agent may not use the money either way; so if he spends it, he is liable.
The shopkeeper is treated like a householder according to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says a changer is like a shopkeeper: if a hekdesh coin fell into his pocket, he is liable once he removes the first coin.
Rabbi Akiva's view, and the Sages say he is liable only after removing the whole pocket, which Rabbi Akiva concedes.
Rabbi Akiva concedes that when he says one coin in this pocket is hekdesh, he is liable only after removing the whole pocket.
When Rav Dimi came, he said Resh Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan what the difference is between the first clause and the latter clause.
Rabbi Yochanan replied that the latter clause concerns one who says this pocket is not exempt from hekdesh.
When Ravin came, he said that pockets of equal value are placed together, and he threw the coins at him.
As we learned in a mishna: one who says one of two pockets is hekdesh, and the larger of them is hekdesh.
Rav said to him that the latter clause concerns one who says this pocket is not exempt from hekdesh.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Pappa raises another contradiction, between the purse ruling here and a mishna about log measures.
The Gemara cites the mishna about one who buys wine from Samaritans, the case that is the basis of the contradiction.
The mishna's procedure: he declares two log to be future teruma and sets aside tithes, then drinks immediately, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon forbid this method, rejecting retroactive designation of the unknown portions.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that the latter clause concerns one who says this purse is not exempt from consecration, meaning the last peruta.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter and of the tractate Me'ilah.
